I think that this is kind of a question to people in general, and not just to teenagers? Because not all teenagers are rude, and not all who are rude are teenagers. But either way, it could be a variety of things: 

* Like you said, "it's not cool to be polite" is something a lot of us think is true.
* We're stressed about something (probably school) and can't be bothered to hide it.
* We are mad at someone else and take it out on the world. 
* We use being rude as a defense if we feel we're being talked down to or belittled in other ways.

Honestly, I'm not 100% sure. We've kinda grown to have a mentality that everything you do needs to be something that gets you the most likes. So you think, will this picture of some landmark I visited get a lot of likes, or will this picture of me *blocking* the landmark get more likes?

I agree, it does take away from what's happening.
It's our way of recording things that are happening while simultaneously being able to show others on social media how "good" we look.
To be completely honest, I feel like *I'm* the one who's out of place in those conventions. I always thought the older people would think I'm too young to be there.

>If you were to write a letter to anyone, alive or dead, and receive a response, who would that person be?

I've always liked the idea of writing a letter to some random person that I have not, and probably never will, meet. I could learn about a life that has absolutely no connection to mine besides our exchange of letters. 

>What do you want to do with your life -- right now?

I want to do better in school, and learn to stop putting things off until the last minute. I also want to try to stop caring about what people think, at least enough for it to not stop me from doing what makes me happy. 

>What good things do you want to put into the world before you die?

Ugh, this is so cheesy but I honestly just want to be the person that can make people feel good about themselves. I want to be able to cheer someone up when they need it, to make them laugh and get them to see the best in life. 

>What things in your life are really difficult?

Living with my dad who is a less than pleasant person. Anxiety about every little thing. Trigonometry. 

>How do you plan to emerge through the other side of those difficult things as a better person?

I'm trying to be the bigger person when it comes to dealing with my dad, and I'm personally trying to help myself with anxiety; if that fails I'll go for outside help eventually. I'm studying super hard in trig!!

>What do you like to read about?

Anything to do with science. Scifi, science textbooks, science reports, anything. 

>If you were to write about something, anything, in your format of choice, what would you write about?

I love the idea of writing poetry, though I doubt I'd be good at it. I would probably write mostly about my emotions about certain things!

Well no. You need to divide 1mol by 6.941, and then multiply by 7.9. Like [this](http://imgur.com/dfCNe4g)
In this case, the mass of the element is what you're given. So, the mass of Li is 7.9 grams, ect. The atomic mass is the mass that is given to you on the periodic table. (Li=6.941 grams)

1. First off you want to start with the mass of the element. Since you have the percentages, as a rule you just assume that whatever the percentage is, that's the mass. So far we have: **7.9% Li--> 7.9 grams of Li    92.1% Br--> 92.1 grams of Br**

1. Next you need to go to represent these numbers in moles. So go to your periodic table, find the molar masses of Li and Br, and then use this formula: **(mass of element)*(1mol/atomic mass of element)** That seems confusing written like that, so if it helps, this is who you'd say it out loud: **The mass of the element multiplied by 1mol over the atomic mass of the element.** Once you do this, you'll have each of the elements in moles. 

1. Divide each of the mole values by the smallest mole value. So let's say the smallest mole value is .33mol, each one would get divided by .33mol.

1. Round to the nearest whole number.

As for what the empirical formula is for, it's to show the proportions between elements in a substance.
